summary: EIMO is an offline clinical decision support system for deep space crews. Using deterministic physics models and four built in browser tests, it provides autonomous medical triage and safety locked emergency care across changing gravity levels when Earth is 14 to 44 minutes away.
details:
What exactly does it do?

EIMO (Engine for In-Flight Medical Operations) is an offline-first medical decision support system for astronauts on long-duration missions. Specifically:

  • It monitors crew health and cabin environment in real time without needing an internet connection to Earth.
  • It detects dangerous spaceflight conditions early, such as high CO2 levels, radiation spikes, noise, and microgravity fluid shifts.
  • It filters out look-alike physical causes before suggesting medical treatments, helping avoid misdiagnosis.
  • It includes interactive in-browser crew checkups (reaction time, hearing, vision, and guided breathing).
  • It saves medical logs and emergency alerts locally so they can sync with Mission Control once communication returns.

How does it work?

The process follows a structured workflow:

  1. Telemetry Input: The system receives live cabin and crew data through interactive sliders, time-step simulation, or mission CSV/JSON files.
  2. Physics & Health Modeling: A deterministic engine calculates how cabin conditions (pressure, CO2, radiation, gravity) affect the astronaut's body systems.
  3. NASA Standards Check: Every reading is evaluated against official NASA-STD-3001, OCHMO, and REMM medical thresholds.
  4. Guided Triage & Checkups: The interface shows clear status alerts, non-pharmacological microgravity procedures, and interactive cognitive, visual, and hearing tests.
  5. Offline Sync Queue: Critical events and logs are stored locally on the device and queued for Store-and-Forward transmission when downlink is available.

What benefits does it have?

Crew Health & Safety: Protects astronauts during deep-space missions where Earth communication has a 4 to 24 minute delay or total blackout, helping catch subtle issues like SANS, hypoxia, or radiation exposure early.

Operational: Gives the crew and onboard medical officer a fast, clear, step-by-step triage tool that works completely offline on any browser or local station laptop.

Scientific & Educational: Connects real space physiology and official NASA standards into an accessible, open-source bilingual (English/Spanish) platform for researchers, students, and mission planners.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, our goal is to provide a verified, ready-to-run open-source prototype that demonstrates autonomous medical monitoring during simulated spaceflight emergencies like CO2 scrubber failures and solar storms. In the long term, we hope EIMO can serve as a foundation for onboard crew health tools in future Lunar and Mars missions where astronauts must rely on local decision support.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Development Tools: Git, GitHub, Node.js, npm, Visual Studio Code
  • Infrastructure and Hosting: GitHub Pages (Static Web App), Uvicorn (Local Server)
  • Backend & API: FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite
  • Frontend & UI: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons, HTML5, CSS3, Web Audio API
  • Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, SQL
  • SI (Super Intelligence) & Development Assistance: Antigravity (Google Gemini) for architecture support, verification, and UI refinement
  • Testing & QA: Pytest, HTTPX
  • Data & Standards Sources: NASA-STD-3001, NASA OCHMO Technical Briefs, U.S. HHS REMM, Canadian Space Agency (CSA) radiation resources, and simulated mission CSV/JSON datasets

How is your project creative?

Instead of just showing raw numbers or static checklists, EIMO turns browser capabilities (Web Audio, interactive vision grids, real-time physics simulation, and offline storage) into practical onboard medical tests that work without cloud servers.

What factors did our team consider?

We prioritized deep-space communication delays (4 to 24 minute one-way delay), astronaut cognitive load during emergencies, bilingual accessibility (English/Spanish), and separating exact NASA standards from simplified simulation models so nothing is misrepresented.
